Listen to this article Share At the heart of Nigeria’s commercial capital lies an interesting paradox. While Lagos State currently ranks as the country’s strongest state for ease of doing business, several persistent issues continue to plague the small and medium-sized businesses operating within its borders. The Presidential Enabling Business Environment Council (PEBEC), in its 2025 Subnational Ease of Doing Business Report, ranked Lagos first nationwide, with a score of 85.6 percent. Among the factors contributing to its rating are transport infrastructure, digital services, land administration, grievance-redress mechanisms, access to credit and a skilled workforce. On the flip side are the issues that continue to taint the state’s business narrative. Multiple taxation has been reported as one of the most persistent, with businesses facing overlapping state, local government, agency and informal levies, particularly in logistics, markets, retail and the informal sector. Against this backdrop, BusinessDay, in partnership with the Organised Private Sector, hosted a town hall conversation with six leading governorship aspirants, who outlined competing manifestos on how they intend to sustain and improve the business environment in Lagos. Their proposals centred largely on reducing the cost of doing business, simplifying government processes, improving infrastructure and creating a more predictable operating environment for private enterprises. For Oluwapamilerin Odunaike of the Labour Party (LP), while the ease of doing business ranking remains impressive, there is a need to simplify the regulatory environment to reduce the incidence of multiple taxation. Odunaike’s proposed solution is to consolidate business-related government services and payments into a single digital platform accommodating business registration, licensing and levy payments. This would reduce the need for enterprises to navigate multiple government agencies. “One of the key items on our manifesto is to ensure that we streamline the taxes and make it simpler, especially for small and medium-sized enterprises, to understand exactly what they are paying. We’re going to open one business portal, your registration, your licensing, your levies, everything comes into that one portal, ” Odunaike said. He also pledged financial and digital assistance for SMEs, alongside the establishment of industry-specific growth centres across the state. Toeing the same line, Laja Adeoye of the Allied Peoples Movement (APM) pointed to the cumbersome government approval processes, and unfriendly tax regime as constraints to business growth. He argued that a more predictable tax system would not only improve profitability for existing businesses but also make Lagos more attractive to new investments and employment creation. His proposal also includes what he called the Lagos State Public and Private Agency, which would serve as a one-stop shop for businesses seeking government approvals and information on their tax obligations. “When you need approval, or you need to do anything with government, you don’t need to move from one ministry to the other,” he said. The proposed agency, he explained, would capture businesses operating in the state and make it easier for them to understand the approvals required and taxes payable without being passed from one government office to another. Funso Doherty of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) focused on the relationship between government accountability and the everyday experience of businesses, arguing that simplifying regulations would need to go hand in hand with stronger public-sector discipline. Like Adeoye’s public and private agency, Funso Doherty proposed establishing a Small Business Ombudsman’s Office to help enterprises navigate government processes and understand their obligations. He also pledged to explore tax rebates and employment tax credits for small businesses that create jobs, arguing that employers who help address unemployment should receive incentives from the government. However, he maintained that reducing harassment by public officials would require tackling the underlying incentives for corruption within the public service. His proposal includes reviewing the salaries, compensation and welfare of public-sector workers, alongside stricter enforcement of the public service code of conduct and prosecution of officials found engaging in criminal activity. “If government doesn’t pay its staff reasonable compensation, they will get that compensation by some other means,” he said, linking inadequate public-sector remuneration to the harassment businesses experience in their daily dealings with government officials. He added that government must also improve the delivery of essential social services, including education, healthcare, affordable housing and public transportation, to reduce the additional costs businesses incur when they have to compensate for gaps in public provision. “The best thing that government can do for you is to govern well,” Doherty said. For Gbadebo Rhodes-Vivour of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), all of the policy reforms would have limited impact if business owners were unaware of their rights and obligations. He proposed deploying teams of business advisers, similar to agricultural extension workers, to engage directly with SME owners and communicate the social contract, explain government policies, provide information on available support, and clarify their tax responsibilities. “Renewing the social contract in the minds of Lagosians and taking that message all the way across Lagos State is going to be something that we’re going to be focused on. We want people to understand what they can expect of the government and be able to hold us accountable to it,” Rhodes-Vivour said. He added that his government would take a firm stance against informal taxation and the harassment of traders and artisans by touts and other non-state actors. He cited instances of traders being forced to make payments at multiple points in markets and tailors having their sewing machines seized, describing such practices as unfair burdens on businesses with little capacity to challenge them. Dr Kadri Obafemi Hamzat of the All Progressives Congress (APC), on the other hand, defended the incumbent administration’s record, noting that Lagos had moved from 19th position in the ease-of-doing-business rankings about six years ago to the top spot, and that the number of taxes had been reduced from 63 to nine, with further harmonisation under consideration. Hamzat, who is the current Deputy Governor of Lagos state, noted that the next phase would be to help businesses start, grow and scale by addressing the infrastructure constraints that increase their operating costs. Citing feedback from the state’s engagement with businesses, Hamzat identified broadband connectivity, reliable power supply and a consolidated payment schedule as key requirements. “What we need to do is to make sure that businesses start, they are able to grow, and they are able to scale. That’s our responsibility, and we make sure to get out of the way for them to do their businesses. So, what do they need? Our survey has shown people need more broadband, power, and that’s what we promise to give to them” He said. Hamzat pledged to increase Lagos’s power generation capacity from its current 900 megawatts to at least 3,500 megawatts within four years through embedded power generation, reducing dependence on the national grid. He also promised the development of four industrial parks and a harmonised payment schedule for businesses. Read also: Hamzat pledges to digitise building approval process to lower housing costs Unlike the other aspirants, Adedeji Doherty of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) approached the question from the perspective of an entrepreneur, arguing that the high cost of operating in Lagos was driven by a combination of taxation, inadequate infrastructure and the broader cost of maintaining a business. He identified poor roads, unreliable power, transportation challenges and high maintenance costs as additional burdens on private enterprises, arguing that these factors made it difficult for businesses to plan and remain profitable. “The high cost of running business in Lagos State is really based on these points that I brought up,” Doherty said, adding that the lack of local government autonomy had further complicated the delivery of basic services, including waste management and other local infrastructure. He questioned the accountability of local government resources, arguing that the funds allocated to councils were not translating into visible improvements in the business environment. For him, improving the operating climate would require addressing these structural governance and infrastructure challenges rather than focusing solely on tax reforms.
